title: The Perfect Tense
description: The perfect active and middle-passive (λέλυκα, λέλυμαι), reduplication, and the perfect as a present state that results from a past action.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html:
The perfect active is the fourth principal part (λέλυκα), the perfect middle and passive the fifth (λέλυμαι). The perfect active adds κα to the reduplicated stem; the middle and passive add the primary middle endings directly to it, with no variable vowel. Reduplication repeats the first consonant of the stem with ε (λέλυκα). A stem beginning with a vowel lengthens it, like the augment (ἤλπικα, ἤτηκα); some stems beginning with two consonants prefix ἐ- (ἔγνωκα, but γέγραφα); φ, θ, χ are reduplicated with π, τ, κ (πεφίληκα, τεθεράπευκα). Unlike the augment, the reduplication stays in every mood, the infinitive and the participle. A final stem vowel is lengthened (μεμαρτύρηκα, μεμαρτύρημαι). Some verbs have a second perfect without κ (γέγονα, ἀκήκοα, ἐλήλυθα).

The Greek perfect has no exact English equivalent: it denotes a present state that results from a past action. ἐγήγερται means he has been raised and is now alive; γέγραπται, it stands written; ἐλήλυθα, I have come and am here. I have loosed and I have been loosed often serve as translations, but the same English may translate an aorist. The pluperfect is rare in the NT and need not be learned.

blocks.caption: Perfect active of λύω
rows: Infinitive λελυκέναι; participle λελυκώς, λελυκυῖα, λελυκός (genitive λελυκότος, λελυκυίας, λελυκότος). Note the accents.

blocks.caption: Perfect middle and passive of λύω
rows: Infinitive λελύσθαι; participle λελυμένος, -η, -ον, declined like ἀγαθός. Note the accents.

blocks.caption: Perfects of this lesson
blocks.html: ἀκήκοα (ἀκούω), βεβάπτισμαι (βαπτίζω), γέγονα (γίνομαι), γέγραφα and γέγραμμαι, γέγραπται (γράφω), ἐγήγερται (ἐγείρω), ἔγνωκα (γινώσκω), ἐλήλυθα (ἔρχομαι), ἑώρακα (ὁράω, used for seeing), τέθνηκα, I am dead (θνήσκω). ἐρρέθην, participle ῥηθείς, is the aorist passive of λέγω: τὸ ῥηθέν, that which was said.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: The augment (ἐ-) belongs only to the indicative of the past tenses; the reduplication (λε-) belongs to the whole perfect: λελυκώς, λελύσθαι. ἔγνωκα and ἔλυσα both begin with ε, but ἔγνωκα is a perfect. γέγονεν (it has come to pass) is from γίνομαι, γεγεννημένος (begotten, born) from γεννάω. ἐγήγερται, he is risen, is a perfect; ἠγέρθη, he was raised, an aorist.
